## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Macchuddānajātaka* (Ja 288) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Jātaka* collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. The story of the present is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivered the teaching concerning a dishonest merchant (*kūṭavāṇija*), opening with the verse beginning *agghanti macchā* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of landholders (*kuṭimbikakula*) during the reign of Brahmadatta in Bārāṇasī [Fausböll 1879]. While waiting with his brother on the banks of the Ganges for a boat, they ate a meal; the Bodhisatta cast the leftover food into the river for the fish and formally dedicated the merit or spiritual profit (*patti*) to the river spirit, who twice derived immediate benefit from the gift [O'Flaherty 1980]. In the concluding identification (*samodhāna*), the Buddha revealed that the dishonest merchant was the younger brother of that time, while he himself was the elder brother, with the merchant subsequently establishing himself in the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) [Fausböll 1879].

Regarding textual parallels, SuttaCentral lists no cross-canonical or external parallels for this jātaka [SuttaCentral]. Automated text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus records six matching Pali passages shared internally with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (volume 2), with its longest shared sequence spanning segments 0.4–1.4 (similarity 0.91), while detecting no cross-language matches above the threshold score in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan corpora [DharmaNexus].
